raw_response.country: India, Indonesia, Thailand, China, Vietnam, Taiwan, Philippines, South Korea, Singapore (11 Asian cities; in-depth flood governance in India, Indonesia, Taiwan)

criterion_notes.c1: Descriptive baseline indicators for basic water services (city-level access to drinking water and access to sanitation) are included among the 25 indicators of the City Blueprint Framework across 11 Asian cities, and World Bank country-level improved water/sanitation access rates are plotted against urban slum percentages (Fig. 5), although the primary empirical governance assessment focuses on flood risk management rather than household/community water or sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines governance factors broadly via the 27-indicator Governance Capacity Framework (GCF) in three cities (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Taipei) and correlates the aggregate Blue City Index (BCI) with the World Bank country-level governance effectiveness index. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT satisfied (no): (1) the empirical GCF analysis is restricted to organisational capacity for flood risk management rather than water or sanitation service access, (2) the 70-city correlation relies on unanalysed macro-governance background (national World Bank governance effectiveness correlated with a composite 25-indicator IWRM index), and (3) narrative Discussion passages on community-based sanitation and slum awareness do not empirically examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) directly governing water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical comparative multi-city indicator assessments (Trends and Pressures Framework and City Blueprint Framework across 11 Asian cities, bivariate correlations across 70 cities, and desk-study plus stakeholder-interview Likert scoring under the Governance Capacity Framework for flood risk in 3 cities).
criterion_notes.c4: Descriptively reports city-level indicator scores for access to drinking water and access to sanitation in the CBF baseline (e.g., Fig. 3 spider plots and text noting low sanitation access in Ho Chi Minh City) and plots national World Bank improved water and sanitation coverage (Fig. 5), though these access measures are not evaluated as outcomes of any legal or administrative mechanism.
criterion_notes.c5: While city-level units of analysis and diagnostic/comparative case-study methods are identifiable, the study does not specify or test an identifiable legal/administrative exposure linked to a water or sanitation service access outcome (the GCF exposure/capacity analysis addresses flood risk, and CBF correlations aggregate 25 heterogeneous water, waste, and climate indicators into a single BCI score).

evidence_quotes.quote: Through the City Blueprint® Approach—an integrated baseline assessment of the urban water cycle—11 Asian cities are assessed. Three cities are selected for an in-depth governance capacity analysis of their challenges with a focus on ﬂoods.
This paper focusses primarily on ﬂood risk management as the detailed assessments of other water-related challenges in the city of Ahmedabad, Bandung and Seoul are published elsewhere
In particular HCMC has low access to sanitation. Moreover, in these cities, wastewater is typically insufﬁciently collected and treated. Drinking water consumption is low and water leakages are high.

In this section, we only provide a short overview and mainly limit ourselves to the governance capacity to deal with the risk of ﬂooding. Table 4 displays a graphic view of the governance capacity proﬁle in these three cities.
the overall BCI score in 70 cities with TPI (r = −0.79), the climate readiness index (r = 0.80), governance effectiveness index (r = 0.80) and GDP per capita (r = 0.70), respectively.

raw_response.exposure: Broad urban IWRM diagnostic indicators, national World Bank governance effectiveness index, and city-level organisational governance capacity for flood risk management (no rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation access)
raw_response.outcome: Composite Blue City Index (25 urban water, waste, and climate indicators including descriptive basic water/sanitation coverage) and Likert-scored flood-risk governance capacity profiles
raw_response.population_and_sample: 11 Asian cities for City Blueprint and Trends and Pressures baseline assessments (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Bangkok, Hohhot, Ho Chi Minh City, Jakarta, Taipei, Tianjin, Manila, Seoul, Singapore; embedded in a 70-city global database), with 3 cities (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Taipei) selected for stakeholder-interview and desk-study flood governance capacity profiles
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper reports descriptive baseline indicator scores for city-level drinking water and sanitation access as part of its 25-indicator City Blueprint Framework across 11 Asian cities, it does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Its in-depth empirical governance assessment (Governance Capacity Framework in Ahmedabad, Bandung, and Taipei) is explicitly limited to flood risk management capacity, and its cross-city governance analysis merely correlates an aggregate 25-indicator IWRM score (Blue City Index) with country-level World Bank governance effectiveness (unanalysed macro-governance background).
raw_response.study_design: Comparative multi-city diagnostic indicator assessment and mixed-methods case-study governance capacity evaluation (secondary indicator compilation, cross-city bivariate correlations, desk study, and stakeholder interviews)
